books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Election returns as published by the Library of Congress, Presidential Election of 1860: A Resource Guide (guides.loc.gov/presidential-election-1860), and the American Presidency Project (presidency.ucsb.edu/statistics/elections/1860). Popular-vote totals differ slightly between sources because of fusion tickets in New York and New Jersey.
stimulus.text:
Results of the presidential election of November 6, 1860. The Electoral College had 303 votes; 152 were needed to win.

| Candidate | Party | Popular votes | Share | Electoral votes |
| Abraham Lincoln | Republican | 1,865,908 | 39.8% | 180 |
| Stephen A. Douglas | Democratic | 1,380,202 | 29.5% | 12 |
| John C. Breckinridge | Southern Democratic | 848,019 | 18.1% | 72 |
| John Bell | Constitutional Union | 590,901 | 12.6% | 39 |

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Which of the following claims is best supported by reading the popular-vote and electoral-vote columns together?

options.text: The candidate with the most popular votes also won the most states.
options.misconception: The table gives no state counts, so it cannot show how many states each candidate won.

options.text: Breckinridge's support was the most evenly spread across the country.
options.misconception: The table gives national totals only, so it cannot show where any candidate's votes were spread.

options.text: Lincoln won the presidency without a majority of the popular vote.
Bell's voters would have backed Douglas if Bell had not run.
options.misconception: The table records what happened, not what voters would have done in a different race.

rationales.A: The table gives no state counts, so it cannot show how many states each candidate won.
rationales.B: The table gives national totals only, so it cannot show where any candidate's votes were spread.
rationales.C: Lincoln's row shows 39.8 percent of the popular vote, under half, beside 180 electoral votes, a clear majority of the 303. Background: winning the presidency took the Electoral College, not a popular majority.
rationales.D: The table records what happened, not what voters would have done in a different race.
rationales.general:
1. Put the two columns side by side for Lincoln: 39.8 percent, and 180 votes.
2. 180 of 303 is a majority of electors, while 39.8 percent is a minority of voters.
3. Background: Lincoln's votes were concentrated in the free states, which held most of the electors.
4. So the table shows a minority president elected by the map.
Remember: compare the two columns, not one alone; the gap between them is the story.
